items.stem: At what point do TypeScript's type annotations take effect?

options.text: At compile time; they are erased and do not exist at runtime
options.rationale: Correct: TypeScript types are checked at compile time and erased in the emitted JavaScript.
Types do not exist at runtime.
Type checking happens during compilation, not in the console.
They are checked by the compiler, not ignored like comments.

items.explanation: Correct: TypeScript types are checked at compile time and erased in the emitted JavaScript.

items.stem: Which TWO are appropriate uses of TypeScript features? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a union type to represent a value that can be one of several specific types
Use generics to write reusable code that preserves type information
options.rationale: Correct: generics keep type safety across reusable code.

options.text: Use any everywhere to avoid compiler errors
options.rationale: any discards type safety and defeats the purpose.

options.text: Rely on types being enforced at runtime

items.explanation: Correct: unions and generics are core typed features; any and runtime enforcement are not.

items.stem: A value has type string | null under strictNullChecks. What must you do before using string methods on it?

options.text: Narrow the type, e.g. check it is not null, so TypeScript knows it is a string
options.rationale: Correct: narrowing removes null from the type before string operations.

options.text: Cast it to any and ignore the warning
options.rationale: Casting to any discards safety and hides real bugs.
Disabling strictness removes the protection rather than handling the case.

options.text: Nothing; TypeScript allows calling string methods on null
options.rationale: Calling string methods on null is an error under strict checks.

items.explanation: Correct: narrowing removes null from the type before string operations.
